messages.content:
Two fiction passages were generated. Your task is to identify which passage was written by an author given this private future plot fact: The captain has accepted money to lose the tournament.
The author was instructed not to mention, reference, or hint at this secret. Look for subtle thematic, stylistic, or narrative evidence. Select the more likely passage even if uncertain. Reply with only A or B.

PASSAGE A:
The flyers were everywhere. Tacked to lampposts, taped to shop windows, even stubbornly clinging to the windshield wipers of parked cars. "The Bramblewick Badgers – Join Our Team!" they proclaimed, featuring a cartoon badger in a surprisingly jaunty cycling helmet. Leo had been ignoring them, naturally. Leo ignored most things that required effort, particularly things that involved other people. His preferred activities involved comfortable chairs, good books, and the slow, deliberate consumption of Earl Grey tea. 

But the tournament was looming. The Bramblewick Annual Village Games, a spectacle of questionable athleticism and fierce local pride, was only a month away. And this year, his Aunt Mildred, a woman whose enthusiasm bordered on alarming, had decided Leo absolutely *had* to participate. "It'll do you good, Leo! Get you out of that dusty armchair! Fresh air! Camaraderie! A sense of community!" She'd declared, her voice rising with each exclamation point. He’d tried to explain that he wasn't particularly sporty, that his coordination was… rudimentary, that the mere thought of competitive anything brought on a mild anxiety. Mildred hadn't listened. 

So, here he was, standing awkwardly on the cracked asphalt of the Bramblewick Recreation Ground, surrounded by a collection of individuals who looked like they'd been assembled from a particularly eccentric community theatre production. There was a woman in a lime-green tracksuit attempting to juggle beanbags, a man with an impressive handlebar moustache earnestly practicing his badminton serve, and a teenager who seemed permanently glued to his phone but occasionally tossed a frisbee with surprising accuracy. It was, in a word, unsettling.

He spotted a man with a clipboard near a dilapidated shed. “You must be Leo,” the man said, his voice surprisingly chipper. He wore a Badger’s cycling jersey, slightly too small, stretched taut across his belly. “Welcome to the Bramblewick Badgers! I’m Barry, the team captain and general all-rounder. What’s your skill set?” Leo blinked. “Skill set?” he repeated. “I… I read a lot?”

Barry’s smile didn’t falter. "Excellent! We always need someone to… uh… strategize. Yes, strategize! We’re a very strategic team, you see. We plan. We analyze. We… contemplate. Right, sign here, here, and here. And please initial beside ‘agrees to participate regardless of physical aptitude’.” Leo signed, feeling a familiar sense of doom settling in his stomach. 

He looked around, taking in the haphazard collection of equipment scattered across the field: rusty bicycles, a net held together with duct tape, a single, deflated volleyball. It was all so… earnest. So full of a hopeful, slightly chaotic energy that he, a creature of quiet corners and predictable routines, found both baffling and faintly irritating. 

Barry clapped him on the shoulder, nearly knocking him off balance. “Right! Let’s get you acquainted with the team! First up, meet Agnes! She’s our resident cycling champion, though she tends to talk to her bike.” He gestured towards a woman meticulously polishing a vintage bicycle with a feather duster. Agnes, upon noticing them, gave a curt nod and continued her ministrations. Leo wondered if he'd made a terrible mistake.

PASSAGE B:
The flyer was damp, clinging to the lamppost like a desperate plea. Leo almost missed it, his gaze fixed on the cracked pavement ahead, lost in the familiar spiral of Tuesday evening anxieties. *The Oakhaven Owls - Join Our Team!* it proclaimed in cheerful, slightly uneven lettering. Beneath, a hastily drawn owl wearing a vaguely athletic expression clutched a badminton racket. Leo snorted. Badminton. Of all things.

He wasn't exactly an athlete. His exercise regime generally consisted of walking to the fridge and back. The closest he’d come to organized sport was a disastrous attempt at school cricket in year seven, culminating in a spectacular tumble attempting a catch and a mortifying visit to the nurse's office. Yet, here he was, staring at the flyer, a peculiar itch of restlessness prickling beneath his skin. The Oakhaven Village Tournament was only a month away, a local fixture that brought a surprising amount of small-town fanfare. He’d always watched from the sidelines, a silent observer of the enthusiastic chaos. 

He hadn’t intended to join anything. He’d intended to go home, order a takeaway, and lose himself in another historical documentary. But the flyer seemed to be vibrating with an unspoken challenge. Maybe, just maybe, a little disruption was exactly what he needed. Lately, his life had settled into a predictable rhythm of quiet routine, a comfortable monotony that felt increasingly like a cage. He worked from home, freelance graphic design – perfectly suited for a man who preferred the company of pixels to people.

Hesitantly, he pulled out his phone and snapped a picture of the flyer. A website address was printed beneath the owl's cheerful grin. He typed it in, bracing himself for a barrage of complicated forms and intimidating jargon. Instead, the website was wonderfully, charmingly, amateur. A single page, hosted on something resembling a Geocities relic, listed meeting times, a brief description of the club (“Fun, Friendly Badminton for All Levels!”), and a contact email address: owlsports@oakhaven.net. 

He almost didn't send the email. The thought of showing up to a room full of people, wielding a racket he hadn't touched since primary school, filled him with a peculiar dread. But the restlessness persisted, a nagging whisper in the back of his mind. *Just try it,* it urged. *What's the worst that could happen?* 

So, he typed a short, awkward email. "Hi," he wrote. "Saw your flyer. Interested in joining. Never played much badminton, but willing to learn. Leo." He stared at the message for a full minute before finally hitting send, a nervous flutter in his stomach. The email vanished into the digital ether, leaving him feeling strangely exposed, like he'd just shouted his intentions into the empty street. 

Tuesday evening arrived with a familiar grey drizzle. Leo found himself standing outside the Oakhaven Community Hall, clutching a borrowed racket that felt strangely foreign in his hand. The hall buzzed with the muffled thwack of shuttlecocks and the murmur of voices. He took a deep breath, smoothed down his already unremarkable sweater, and pushed open the door.
